title: When Should I Replace My Air Conditioner?
h1: When Should I Replace My Air Conditioner? What to Weigh First
description: Age, repair history, refrigerant type, comfort and energy use all factor into AC replacement. Here is how to decide between one more repair and a new system.
quick_answer: Consider replacing your air conditioner when it is getting old and needs a major repair, uses an outdated refrigerant, breaks down repeatedly, no longer keeps the house comfortable or is driving energy bills up. If the system is newer and the repair is minor, repairing it is usually the better call.
body:
Very few air conditioners fail all at once. More often, the repairs get closer together, the bills creep up and the upstairs never quite cools off. The hard part is deciding when one more repair stops making sense. Here's how we help homeowners think it through.

How old is your system?

Age alone doesn't mean a system needs replacing, but it changes the math. A well-maintained central AC often runs for many years, while one that was installed poorly, sized wrong or skipped maintenance may wear out sooner. Coastal units can also age faster because salt air corrodes coils and electrical connections.

You can usually find the manufacture date on the label of the outdoor unit. If the system is getting up there in years and facing a big repair like a compressor or outdoor coil, replacement deserves a serious look.

Is the repair worth it?

A simple way to frame it: compare the repair cost to the value left in the system. A capacitor or contactor on a newer system is an easy yes. A compressor on an older system with a history of refrigerant leaks is a different story.

Questions to ask yourself:

  • Has the system needed more than one significant repair in the last couple of years?
  • Is the current repair a major component like the compressor, coil or blower motor?
  • Will other parts of similar age be likely to fail soon?
  • Would the repair money go a meaningful way toward a new system?

If you're answering yes to most of those, putting the money toward a replacement often makes more sense.

What refrigerant does it use?

Many older systems use R-22, which hasn't been produced or imported in the US since 2020. What's left is limited and costly, so recharging an R-22 system after a leak can be expensive. Newer systems use refrigerants like R-410A, and equipment built today is moving to lower-impact refrigerants. If your system still runs on R-22 and has a leak, replacement is usually the practical path.

Is the house still comfortable?

Comfort problems can point to a system that's no longer up to the job, though they can also come from ducts, insulation or thermostat placement. Watch for:

  • Rooms or floors that stay several degrees warmer than the rest of the house.
  • A system that runs all afternoon on hot inland days and still can't hold the setpoint.
  • Sticky, humid air even when the AC is running.
  • More dust or noise than there used to be.

Before replacing anything, it's worth checking the ducts and attic insulation. A new system on leaky ducts won't fix comfort problems on its own. Sometimes duct repair or added insulation solves the issue for less.

Are your energy bills climbing?

As systems age, they usually lose efficiency. Dirty coils, worn motors and small refrigerant leaks all make the system run longer. If your summer bills have gone up without a change in how you use the AC, the system may be the reason. Newer systems with higher SEER2 ratings and variable-speed operation can cut operating costs, especially in homes that run cooling a lot.

What should you plan for when replacing?

If replacement makes sense, a few decisions come with it:

  1. Sizing. Ask for a load calculation rather than matching the old unit. Many older systems were oversized or undersized from the start.
  2. System type. Consider whether a heat pump, a furnace and AC pair, or ductless mini-splits fit your home best.
  3. Ducts. Have them inspected for leaks, crushed runs and proper sizing.
  4. Electrical. Some homes need panel or circuit work to support a new system or heat pump.
  5. Thermostat. A new system may benefit from a compatible thermostat that controls staging or variable speed.

Planning ahead also helps. Replacing a system in spring or fall, before it fails in the middle of a heat wave, gives you time to compare options instead of making a rushed decision.

When you're weighing it, we'll look at the system, explain what's wrong and give you the cost of repair alongside the options for replacement. If repair is the sensible choice, we'll say so. You can read about our air conditioning repair and replacement service, and replacement estimates are free.
faqs: How long does a central air conditioner last?

It varies with maintenance, installation quality, sizing and location. Coastal units exposed to salt air and inland units that run hard all summer may wear sooner. Regular tune-ups help any system last longer.
Should I replace my AC and furnace at the same time?

Often it makes sense, especially if both are older, because the indoor coil and outdoor unit need to be matched and the work can be done in one visit. If the furnace is newer and in good shape, replacing only the AC can work.
Is it worth repairing an R-22 air conditioner?

Small repairs that do not involve refrigerant can still make sense. If the system has a leak and needs a recharge, the limited supply of R-22 makes replacement the more practical choice in most cases.
Will a new AC lower my energy bills?

A newer, properly sized system is usually more efficient than an aging one, especially if the old unit is worn or leaking. How much you save depends on how much you run the AC and the condition of your ducts and insulation.
